Jerome Kagan: The Nature of the Child. Published by Basic Books, 1984. Hardback, £15.85. Also by Harper and Row. Paperback, £4.95.

Jill Hodges

Jill Hodges

Jill Hodges  

This book by Harvard University's Professor of Developmental Psychology examines a number of major themes in the study of children's development. It begins with an over-arching essay on “Guiding Themes in Human Development”, and goes on to cover the topics of infancy, connectedness versus discontinuity in development, the establishment of morality, the emotions, the development of thought, and the role of the family.

These are issues which could hardly be more relevant for us as child psychotherapists, and expectations on beginning the book are high. The assumptions which structure how we think about, or even perceive, what we observe, are part of a theoretical framework we generally take for granted; the opportunity to step back and examine the framework itself, its differences and commonalities with other approaches, is very inviting. So too is the sense that the book will provide an up-to-date integration of current research and thinking in several crucial areas.

Not surprisingly, these over-high expectations are not fulfilled, though the second is fulfilled to a greater degree than the first. And not surprisingly in a book on psychology, Freud and psychoanalytic ideas are very little discussed (or acknowledged). In Kagan's account, they tend to be written off into something of an historical hinterland from which they still exercise a (questionable) influence on some current modes of thinking; and they are sometimes inaccurately presented.

Kagan argues that greater consideration should be given, in various areas of attachment, emotional development, self-awareness, etc., to the underlying maturationally based cognitive changes which make such development possible. However, this makes the book sound more monotonous, more mechanistic, and less interesting than it is in reality. (Despite the emphasis on cognition, he maintains, for instance, that feeling, not logic, sustains conscience, in opposition to Kohlberg.)

The chapters are of uneven value, at least to this reader. The final chapter on the role of the family is perhaps the weakest, more prescriptive in its tone and personal in its view of what the American family needs to give the American child, and disappointingly lacking in much research, unlike the other chapters.

[[RunningHead]]

Julia Segal: Phantasy in Everyday Life. Published by Pelican, 1985. Paperback £2.95.

Julia Segal's aim-is to provide “professionals and the wider general public” with an introduction to Kleinian ideas — “a psycho-analytic approach to understanding ourselves”. As far as I am aware there is no other book that addresses itself in this way to a non-analytic audience.

The author takes the concept of phantasy as her central theme and, having looked at phantasy itself, sets out to explore, in a series of chapters, how our unconscious phantasy life can affect our view of the world and how we react in various settings: in our Family Life, at Work, in Relationships and so on. This constitutes the bulk of the book.

She is clearly well versed in Kleinian ideas and her account is thorough and systematic. It is also copiously illustrated with examples from her own experience which help bring to life what can otherwise be quite difficult concepts. The examples taken from everyday life are particularly helpful and quite a few of these involve children and have the advantage that they might encourage the reader to take children's ideas and feelings more seriously and thoughtfully. The examples from her own counselling practice were less satisfactory, some were too sketchy to be convincing, others rather too “neat”. They give the impression that simply being able to name the phantasy that is operative can bring an instant resolution of whatever the problem may be. They thereby leave the non-analytic reader with a misleading sense of the analytic process.

One risk with an introductory work of this kind is that the reader may feel tempted to go in for do-it-yourself analysis, misapplying half digested ideas. Julia Segal warns the reader against just such an eventuality but she fails to make it sufficiently clear how the insights she is offering can be applied without falling into this trap and my feeling is that the overall effect of the book will be to encourage the reader into precisely this error.

[[RunningHead]]

The Boundary between Psychotherapy and Therapeutic Teaching**

John Woods

John Woods

21 Hillfield Road
London
NW6 1QD

John Woods  

Education and psychotherapy make a complex, and in some ways contradictory, combination. The therapist who works in a special school has to adapt the technique that was developed, and is more usually applied, in outpatient settings; the educational goals of the school have to be respected, and there is the danger that these swamp those of the therapist. For the teacher there is correspondingly a necessity to include a therapeutic dimension to the work with the disturbed child; this can militate against the social expectations of education and get the teacher into difficulties with the child. Given also the frequently intractable nature of problems presented by these children in special schools, it should come as no surprise that teacher and therapist find themselves sometimes at odds with each other around the “emotionally and behaviourally disturbed” child. I shall attempt here to show how this conflict is not only a function of professional rivalry or territoriality, but also can be seen as an expression of the child's difficulty in integrating inner and outer realities. When, for example, the worker feels threatened in his or her professional identity, this may be a clue to feelings that the child himself is unable to deal with, such as terrors of castration or annihilation. The steps by which workers become frustrated, ineffective and divided can be retraced to the child's disturbance. If both the child and the adults are nearer to the source of their difficulty with each other then they may also be closer to the possibility of change for the child.

Clinical Material

I was asked recently, as the child psychotherapist in a day special school, if I would see a boy about whom there was a great deal of concern expressed, particularly by his teacher. Ian, as I shall call him, was uncommunicative, isolated, resentful, and given to bouts of violent rage. The attempt to find a psychotherapeutic view of this child's difficulties illustrates some of the problems and opportunities of the therapist's work in the school setting.

Towards Integration and Independence: A Four-Year-Old Boy's use of Thirteen Months of Psychotherapy

Barbara Gaffney

Barbara Gaffney

33 Hanover Road
London, NW 10

Barbara Gaffney  

Introduction

In this paper I will describe thirteen months of work with Peter, a boy who was four and a half years old when we first met. Through his treatment I became especially interested in his use of a blanket which he called “Baa”. It served many functions which I shall consider later. This treatment also raised the technical question about the appropriateness of reconstruction in the treatment of a young child.

The referral

Peter's parents, Mr. and Mrs. X, first contacted the psychiatry department on the recommendation of their GP one March. Mrs. X was pregnant and they were worried about Peter's aggressive and disruptive behaviour. The health visitor was concerned that Peter might be hyperactive. However, several months passed before they requested further help. This was after the birth of a third child in the family.

During assessment, in November a year and a half later, Peter's parents described his unpredictable outbursts, where he would suddenly kick or punch his younger sister and his parents. So far he had been protective towards the new baby. At times they could see a conflict building up in him until he became “out of control”. He was generally protective towards his mother but “horrible” when also with other children; she often felt driven to smack him. Peter was more contained if his father was around.

Mrs. X felt Peter was unhappy. He told her that he had feelings and “did not know where they came from”. He was reluctant to go to school or out to play and had no friends. He clung to his mother saying that he wanted to stay with the family for “always”, and said he wanted to get back inside her.

Mrs. X had been concerned for some time but finally sought help when, after Peter had been at school for a term, his teachers confirmed her fears. The teacher described him as anxious and preoccupied with death, unable to sustain play or leaning, at times disruptive and bossy. Mr. X was less worried as he remembered his own difficulties early on at school which he felt he had grown out of.

The Sado-Masochistic Phantasies of Two Adolescent Boys Suffering from Congenital Physical Illnesses

Alex Dubinsky

Alex Dubinsky

3 Kemplay Road London N.W. 3.
London

Alex Dubinsky  

Tim and Jack are two adolescent boys who I have seen for once a week psychotherapy in a boarding school. Both are physically handicapped. Both were caught in a massive use of protective identification by their fascination for the scenes of cruelty which they phantasised happening inside Mother's body. These two boys felt that the congenital illnesses, which had actually affected them in the womb, and the subsequent damage and anguish they have suffered, were the result of sado-masochistic conflict taking place in the interior of Mother's body.

Tim's phantasies of invasion

Tim, who was just fifteen when he started therapy, was referred because it was felt he failed to develop emotionally.

A severe congenital heart defect puts his life in danger. He is able to walk only short distances. His face is cyanosed and when, instead of using his wheelchair, he walks to his sessions, he gasps for breath. An operation to remedy the heart defect when he was four caused a blood clot which resulted in his losing the use of one arm, and having a somewhat limp leg. Six months before Tim's birth, his father underwent dental surgery and died under the anaesthetic. Tim's mother remarried and he has two younger half-siblings who live at home.

The session I will now describe took place after six months of work, and gives a vivid portrait of Tim, in that early phase of his therapy.

Tim had complained the previous week that because of therapy he only attended the first fifteen minutes of the woodcraft lesson. He talked of this lesson as he came in and then, to my dismay, told me how “that girl” in the school office had gathered together all my patients, in order to check the times of their session. “The girl” was actually the school secretary, a mature lady. According to Tim she had asked him whether he was satisfied with the time of his session. He had said he was not and had been told to discuss this with me. Instead he had arranged to swap times with another patient, but he then realized he would be missing his art lesson. Indeed, Tim's greed, which was often in evidence, meant that he wanted everything: his lesson, his session and the other boys' sessions. He then went on to tell me of what he calls his “accidents.

[[RunningHead]]

Solving the Mystery of Monsters: Steps Towards the Recovery from Trauma

Juliet Hopkins

Juliet Hopkins

The Tavistock Clinic
London

Juliet Hopkins  

Freud wrote in 1909 that “a thing which has not been understood inevitably reappears; like an unlaid ghost it cannot rest until the mystery has been solved and the spell broken.”

This paper is concerned with solving the mystery and breaking the spell which binds children who have become the victims of trauma. It illustrates how psychotherapy can free children from the worst effects of trauma by enabling them to accept both the reality of the traumatic event and of the feelings which it aroused. In this way both these elements of the traumatic experience can be integrated and a start made in the process of recovery. I give examples from the psychotherapy of two children and consider the stages by which recovery from trauma takes place, and discuss the role of the child psychotherapist in facilitating it.

In defining trauma I follow Freud's statement of 1926: “The essence of a traumatic situation is an experience of helplessness on the part of the ego in the face of accumulation of excitation, whether of external or internal origin.” This definition links the specific external event with internal psychic conditions and indicates the shattering, devastating and generally overwhelming effect of a trauma. Spontaneous recovery from such an event is possible, though commonly subsequent development is altered and takes a pathological course, as it did in the case of the two children whose clinical material I want to present. These children had both been subjected to recurrent traumas from their earliest years. They both had serious learning difficulties, and they were both preoccupied with monsters to the exclusion of all other interests. But I have selected them mainly because of the different response to trauma which each represents: one child retained detailed knowledge of the traumas but had no awareness that these events had been the cause of any suffering; the other child had retained no conscious knowledge of the traumas but remained overwhelmed by the distressing emotions which these events had aroused.

Editorial

Deborah Bandler

Deborah Bandler

Deborah Bandler  

The last issue of the Journal marked the end of Mrs. Lisa Miller's term as Editor. We would like to thank her for her long and hard work, the high standards she set, and the generous and enthusiastic spirit with which she headed the Editorial Team.

Our thanks are due also to other members of the Committee who have finished their terms, and to Mrs. Kerry Kelly Novick who, up until this year, worked for a number of years as Corresponding Editor, U.S.A.

This issue is thus the first of an Editorial Committee that is both re-grouped and new. Just as the membership of the Committee reflects the various schools of thought within the Association, we hope that the Journal will continue to represent the various interests and points of view of Child Psychotherapists. These interests and points of view are indicative of the spirit of continuity and change within our profession. Individual psycho-analytic and psychotherapeutic work remains the mainstay of our profession: there is also increasing interest in and need for applied work. Examples of both the former and the latter are seen in this issue.

In future issues we hope to realise two projects, begun with the previous Team. We would still like to introduce a correspondence section, consisting of responses to published papers, and in this way add an element of active dialogue to the Journal. The aims of the second project are to increase awareness and knowledge of work done abroad, as well as to foster links with overseas members. We are thus asking eight Association members from six different countries to act as Overseas Representatives for the Journal. The task will be to encourage submission of papers to the Journal, and the enthusiastic response thus far perhaps indicates both the timeliness of and the need for such an innovation.

Children and Institutions II: The Professional and the Institution

Trevor Hartnup

Trevor Hartnup

4 Sutton Lane
London, W4

Trevor Hartnup  

Introduction

This paper examines the function of the structure and organisation of institutions and their relevance to the clinical work. It discusses the positive contribution which they can make to the joint treatment of the child by a staff team, and some of the dangers inherent in professional relationships in institutions. It illustrates some of the forces which seek to dismantle or alter the formal structures, and how careful attention to these institutional processes can bring clinical rewards. Similarly, it considers how thoughtful use of the physical environment contributes to making the setting therapeutic.

The examples spring from my own experience and from what my colleagues have shared with me about their experience. I am very grateful to them for sharing their thoughts and feelings with me, and for their permission to present in this paper some of the insights which have emerged from our discussions.

In day and residential units staff members work in teams and each member of staff has to find ways of working with his colleagues, whether they are from the same or different disciplines. It may be that most of us come into this kind of work because we are interested in working with children and families. This is the focus of our training, at any rate. However, there is no intrinsic reason why professionals who are skilled at work with clients should be good at working with each other, or have a talent for harnessing the therapeutic potential of institutional living. In fact, only too often the institution is apparently ignored, taken for granted or experienced by clients and staff alike as an unwelcome third party in their relationship. Of course, it is reasonable to assume that the skill of working with colleagues and an appreciation of the role of the institution will tend to develop more readily in work situations where they are already valued.

Children who come to day and residential units usually do so because they and their parents are under such stress and strain that it becomes impossible to care for them adequately in their own homes, or because someone else is very concerned about the child's development and the care he is receiving. Sometimes it appears that in addition to having his own difficulties which pertain to his own internal world, the child is having to deal with parents who are unable to look after themselves or their own relationship and emotional lives adequately. It goes without saying that in institutions we attempt to ensure that we minimise the extent to which we expose the child to our own personal difficulties, and our problems in our relationships with our colleagues.

Aggressively Abused Children

Erna Furman

Erna Furman

2689 Colchester Road
Cleveland
Ohio 44106 U.S.A.

Erna Furman  

The dictionary, as well as common usage, defines aggressive abuse as maltreatment and we usually think of it as inflicting bodily pain and harm. In the same context, however, the dictionary also defines abusing as “performing an established unjust practice” (The Concise Oxford Dictionary, 1946) which implies social and cultural variations. In this country, with its heterogenous groups and rapidly changing value systems, a necessary and legitimate educational means of discipline to one may be a form of abuse to another. For example, parents often ask nursery school teachers to spank their children and criticize preschools for refraining from physical punishment. Indeed, one of the preschool or day-care teacher's first tasks with parent and child frequently focuses on clarifying such differences between home and school rules and assuring them that the nursery will provide order and safety without paddling.

From elementary school on, physical punishment of children is permitted by law. In contrast, the law protects adult offenders from any form of bodily discipline, excepting the recent reintroduction of capital punishment. In regard to children, however, the law is far from clear cut. While allowing physical punishment, it not only prohibits aggressive abuse but often extends the term. For example, according to Ohio State (Rev. Code Ann. 2151.42.1) we must consider “any wound, injury, disability, or condition of such a nature as to reasonably indicate abuse or neglect of such child.” This purposeful vagueness covers a large number of conditions which may be viewed and interpreted differently by different people, makes it hard to draw the line between child rearing practices and abuse or to pinpoint exactly when parental handling constitutes neglect or significant mental and bodily harm.

A psychological definition includes not only maltreatment resulting in bodily hurt and physical and/or emotional neglect but a whole host of more subtle forms of child-adult interactions which may nevertheless be very damaging to the growing personality. Shengold (1979) used the word “soul murder” to describe these kinds of child abuse and deprivation. He started his article with a patient's memory of his whole family sitting at the dinner table, each member served a banana for dessert. The father got up, manually squashed each banana except his own, then resumed his seat. Nobody protested, everyone silently ate up their mess. Past intimidation had been so forceful that no child even whimpered, much less complained. I have in mind many less concrete but equally devastating examples of helplessly being made into a nothing or of being teased or confused or falsely blamed to the point of having to surrender one's feeling, knowing, functioning self — the essence of abuse.

Gregorio Kohon (ed): The British School of Psychoanalysis: The Independent Tradition. Published by Free Association Books, 1986. Hardback, £25.00. Paperback, £9.95.

Anne Hurry

Anne Hurry

Anne Hurry  

This book has been well reviewed in several publications, but deserves special mention in our journal because of its potential importance to child psychotherapists. Most of us have been trained as “classical Freudians” or “Kleinians” and, Winnicott apart, our knowledge of the Independent Group comes mainly from our own reading and discussion, or from further training.

Here for the first time is a book which shows the variety and spontaneity of thinking which can occur in the Independent Group. At the same time the underlying assumptions of independent analysts emerge in a way which allows the reader to integrate them constructively as he comes upon them from different points of view.

Kohon's introduction, in which he sets out the history of the psychoanalytic movement in Great Britain, is masterly: clear, thoughtful and non-polemical (in contrast to the somewhat grumpy tone of Martin James' paper on “Premature Ego Development”). This introduction could be particularly helpful to those puzzled students who enquire “What is the A, the B, the Middle Group?”

There follow some twenty papers by independent analysts, the majority dating from 1975 on, but going back as far as 1958 with Rycroft's classic “Enquiry into the Function of Words in the Psychoanalytical Situation”. There are four sections: on early environment; on the psychoanalytic encounter; on regression and the psychoanalytic situation; on female sexuality.

The section headings indicate the main areas in which independent analysts have made their major contributions. But each section provides much more than indicated by the heading. The section on “Early Environment” for instance, contains Khan's paper on “The Concept of Cumulative Trauma” and Winnicott's on “Fear of Breakdown”. But it also contains Padel's (1985) “Ego in Current Thinking” which will surely become a classic. Padel gives a scholarly critique of psychoanalytic thinking on the ego and the self, and an illuminating discussion on the nature and role of identification in the development of the ego. He notes that, “Each one of us has sat on mother's knee to smile at father and been held over father's shoulder to make eyes at mother. In that early three-person situation identification and object-relation occur together and facilitate one another”. He concludes “Identification is not the consequence of internalising but accompanies or precedes it. By identifying we internalise a field, a situation, or a relationship”. I have found that to view identification in this way, rather than to think of identification as being with an object or part-object, subtly alters my hearing of clinical material, and my understanding of such defenses as role reversal, identification with the aggressor, passive into active and so on. Such “defenses” can be seen less as devices utilised in order to avoid pain, and more as ways of being which may be excessively used, distorted, to that same end. This has obvious clinical implications.

Children and Institutions I: The Child and the Professional

Trevor Hartnup

Trevor Hartnup

4 Sutton Lane
London, W4

Trevor Hartnup  

Introduction

This paper attempts to pick out the specifically institutional dimension of the interactions between the children and professional staff of institutions catering for troubled children and adolescents. I use the word “institution” to mean both a physical place (building, rooms, furnishings etc.) and a social system in which people are in formal (and informal) relationships with each other. I concentrate upon the meaning of the institution to the child and the role of the professional who tries to provide conditions in which the child can make sense of his experience.

In addressing the question of what institutions mean to children, I have used theories derived from psychoanalysis and from the study of organisations, and brought them to bear upon the experiences of psychotherapists working in institutions. Although my examples come from the setting of psychotherapy, I am not addressing the subject of specialised treatments which may take place in institutions, but rather the general therapeutic setting of institutional life which may support whatever specialised treatments are available within it. The client group is an important aspect of a child's experience in day and residential units, but it lies outside the scope of this paper.

It is difficult to conceive of a child's experience of an institution except in terms of his relationships with the staff, who bring to the relationship the stamp of the place and the social system in which they work. One could say that the child's experience of the institution is mediated by the staff. On the one hand, the professionals find themselves having to take account of the institution, its organisation, its task and its resources, and the dynamics of small and large groups in the various groupings of staff. On the other hand, they are beset by the problems of the children, their deprivations and traumas which evoke sympathy and the wish to help, and their confusing and exasperating behaviour and rejections, which make staff feel helpless and angry. To these pressures, the professional member of staff brings his training and his personal capacity for processing his experience. This capacity depends upon tolerating uncertainty and strong feelings, linking his observations together into a meaningful form without prematurely imposing a meaning upon them. It is part of his job to help the child make sense of the institution, and to marshal the resources of the institution in response to his understanding of the child.

The Building of an Obsessional Neurosis during the Analytic Treatment of an Obsessional Sado-Masochistic Adolescent Boy

Pat Radford

Pat Radford

Maresfield Gardens
London N.W.3.

Pat Radford  

Anna Freud noted that, at his diagnostic assessment, Ronnie, a 1312 year old boy, was not a true obsessional neurotic. After 412 years' analysis I can say that he is not cured of his conflicts nor is his obsessional neurosis fully confirmed. This paper sets out to try to distinguish between the phenomena present in the clinical material and the theoretical implications.

I must therefore try to assess if the difficult, often despairing, frequently tortuous analytic treatment, has clarified the state of Ronnie's mental health. Have I understood the significance of his symptoms in relation to a specific diagnosis? Had there been any permanent shift in his psychic structure? Has the ongoing, collusive, sado-masochistic relationship between the parents and himself proved too great a barrier to complete internalisation of his conflicts? Has his ambivalence remained too out of balance to allow libidinal and aggressive fusion? Has his ego remained too split to provide an economic defence structure or to synthesise his bi-sexual contradictions? Has his adolescent developmental process worked against the re-alignment of his psychic forces? Has the technique been inadequate, the analyst's fight to avoid sadomasochistic involvement too unsuccessful and the counter transference too great to enable Ronnie to gain insight into his internal world and resolve his conflicts?

Undoubtedly little has changed in his parents' attitudes in spite of the P.S.W.'s painstaking work with them. I shall not try to discuss this, noting only that the parental pathology and attitudes prevalent at the diagnostic stage have basically remained the same.

Ronnie, aged 412, was taken by his mother to a Child Guidance Clinic because of his appallingly bad relationship with her. The round-faced curly-headed cherub, as described by his psychotherapist, was hard to reconcile with his mother's description. She saw him as torturing his parents, endlessly talking, frequently grunting, unable to occupy himself or take initiatives. His infancy had been disturbed. The only child, he was conceived three months after his 45 year old mother had had a severe miscarriage. She was apprehensive throughout the pregnancy, not only of having a Mongoloid child, but also of the loss of her husband's love. The deterioration in their relationship she felt was totally the result of his domination by his “malignant” mother. The birth was easy, but from seven days old, Ronnie had screaming fits for no reason apparent to the paediatricians or his Health Visitor mother. It is not known how rigidly Mrs. C. functioned as a mother.

Observations On a Case of Bulimia

Richard Rusbridger

Richard Rusbridger

27 Normanby Road
London NW10

Richard Rusbridger  

In this paper I describe some aspects of the psychopathology of a bulimic patient who was 19 when she started treatment. I treated her in psychotherapy three times a week for three and a half years. In particular, I wish to stress the contribution made by this patient's extreme intolerance, both of psychic emptiness and, as importantly, of mental pain. This may indicate a phenomenon of general importance in bulimia. For clarity I have concentrated on the first year of the therapy, where the gradual unfolding of her difficulties, and of the ways in which she had tried to cope with them can be seen.

Anorexia nervosa has received a good deal of psycho-analytic attention (see particularly Tustin 1958; Pines, M. 1973; Kalucy 1973; and Thomä 1977); its counterpart, bulimia, (Fairburn 1982, 1983) somewhat less (notable exceptions being Sprince 1984 and Thorner 1969). In connection with both syndromes, psycho-analytic writers have stressed the patients' experience of emptiness, apparently resulting from traumatic experiences of separation from, and inconstancy in, the primary caring object. As will be seen, this was certainly evident in my patient. Indeed “emptiness” seems an inadequate word to describe the piercing and biting quality of the experience in which, as Bion (1962) and O'Shaughnessy (1964) observe, an absent object can be experienced as a very present and persecuting one. But in addition to that, and arising from it, my patient showed an inability to tolerate or think about any pain, including that arising from separation. I hope to show that, in order to understand the nature of the gorging and vomiting in bulimia, both the search to fill an inner emptiness and the extreme intolerance of mental pain need to be taken into account.

Concepts of the Inner World in George Eliot's Work

Margot Waddell

Margot Waddell

5 Cardozo Road
London N7

Margot Waddell  

“The beginning of an acquaintance, whether with persons or things is to get a definite outline of our ignorance.”

This comment of George Eliot's well describes the kind of unlearning that may have to take place before knowledge of a different kind can be acquired and meaningful change occur. It is a painful, uncertain and often confusing process. It involves the relinquishment of preconceptions, of acquired ways of thinking, of the defensive structures of bodies of knowledge and conventional learning, used all too easily merely as bulwarks against significant change, as tyrannical structures of thought, demanding acquiescence out of ambition or fear. Such structures engender inferiority and a decreasing capacity to think for onself.

It was a curious position for a woman of such profound learning and powerful intellect, yet it was deeply felt. The novels fundamentally challenged the current tenets of scientific rationality to which, with a part of herself, George Eliot gave full credence. In place of that positivistic way of thinking her works offer an alternative mode, much more readily recognisable to those familiar with the struggle to acquire the capacity to learn, to acknowledge and bear the truth about themselves — a struggle which lies perhaps at the heart of the developmental or psychoanalytic experience.

The dual moment of what A.N. Whitehead characterised as the mid-nineteenth-century “distracted mind” is well caught in George Eliot's prepublication review of Darwin's On the Origin of Species. She says: “We have been reading Darwin's book on ‘Origin of Species’: it makes an epoch, as an expression of his thorough adhesion, after long years of study, to the DOCTRINE OF DEVELOPMENT … So the world gets on step by step towards brave clearness and honesty! But to me the development theory and all other explanations of processes by which things came to be, produce a feeble impression compared with the mystery that lies under the processes.”

The extent to which most of our lives are dedicated to the evasion of what “lies under the processes”, to the substitution of counterfeit values, and worthy preoccupations which may assuage guilt, service, in part satisfy, but ultimately touch on very little, is a lesson profoundly painful in the learning — one which many of us do not willingly undergo. The fact is that most of us can bear very little reality.

The Monster and the Ballet Dancer: A Four-Year-Old's View of Sexual Abuse

Margaret Hunter

Margaret Hunter

Tavistock Clinic
120 Belsize Lane
London, NW3

Margaret Hunter  

Introduction

Working with children in care can be a traumatic experience in itself for those working and caring for them. These children have often had so many hurtful and indigestible experiences that it is difficult for the carers to absorb the painful facts of their short existences, let alone allow some room for the children to share their view of these happenings. When working with these children, I am constantly reminded of how we push out of our minds their sad histories. At the same time we cannot, nor should we, be so mindful of the past that we make our present immediate contact with them devoid of spontaneity. Still, I cannot help noticing that, most frequently, the workers — myself included — have a strong tendency to operate exclusively in the present. At case reviews or anytime when a child's behaviour is discussed, one gets easily caught in perplexity and a sense of the mysteriousness of childish actions when all too often the reason for the actions is blindingly clear from the child's past history.

“She makes such a fuss at bedtime”, we say with exasperation, for at that moment we have split off the knowledge, discussed at the last meeting, that mother used to leave her alone at night locked in her room. And if we remember, we can then feel guilty and inadequate. This is never more true than with sexually abused children. Sexual abuse of a child is a fact so riven with anxieties that our own intense feelings can throw us off balance. In social services and child guidance clinics there are an increasing number of sexually abused children referred. I have noticed that it is difficult to steer a course between an obsessive sort of preoccupation with the sad facts of their sexual abuse—a sort of sensationalism which can serve to defend us against anxiety—and an ignoring or dismissing of a child's exploitation which really amounts to denial. We waiver too between over-identification where we can leave ourselves at the mercy of our own feelings of anger and retaliation, and denying the possibility of identification at all.

Lisa Miller

Lisa Miller

Lisa Miller  

Meltzer has not settled down at his desk to write a book called “Clinical Applications of Bion's Ideas”, as the sub-title has it. The integration of this book springs from something different. In one sense it is a record of continuing work: we are offered a bunch of loosely-gathered papers composed over a number of years, a period of time straddling the publication of Meltzer's last book, Dream-Life, reviewed here in 1985. The level of these collected studies is uneven and they were produced for varying purposes and audiences.

One thing unifies them. They are a record of the effect which Bion's ideas have had upon Meltzer's way of thinking and working: they form an account of what Meltzer has made of Bion. So we are given an impression of one of the very processes to which Bion and Meltzer are always drawing our attention, the process whereby we assimilate a new experience and make it into a part of ourselves. Meltzer has literally worked on Bion's ideas: they have fuelled him and he has processed them. The “studies” of the title have their origins in the different aspects of his working life. They come from supervising, leading seminars, delivering papers, analysing patients and, clearly though implicitly, from a constant working process of self-scrutiny. Meltzer is delighted to recognise illumination wherever it occurs, and he displays other workers' clinical material with enthusiasm and generosity.

This in itself may be encouraging to those of us who feel we need all the help we can find to aid our digestion of Bion's ideas. Though Meltzer addresses some of these in detail (the reversal of alpha function, for instance), much of the value of the book seems to me to lie in the way it helps us in the process of addressing and re-addressing some of the powerful fundamental preoccupations behind Bion's work: his concept of change and growth; the relationship between group mentality and individual identity, and, linked with both these, the questions of thinking and thought, and the psychotic areas of the personality.

Dilys Daws  

Samantha, a nine year old patient, fell asleep during a session. I let her sleep for a few minutes, then woke her, and sat next to her as she collected herself. It was nearly time to go, and I talked briefly of what I felt was her depression and her need to block out the pain of what we had earlier talked about in the session.

Two hours later, Samantha's mother, Mrs. H. phoned and asked “Did you hypnotize Samantha?” The unexpectedness of the question, about a technique so outside my own practice of psychotherapy, nearly prompted me into a facetious reply, but in fact I answered seriously that I had not done so, that I did not know how to hypnotize, that, as far as I knew, no-one in our building used hypnosis, and that if it were used on children it would be with parents' knowledge and consent. Mrs. H. had only my word to go on, but appeared satisfied by this interchange. The question remains, how is a responsible parent to evaluate what goes on between a professional and their child, when the professional insists on working in privacy and confidentiality that excludes the parent?

In the H. family's case the difficulty was real. Samantha was referred for depression which had started at the time of her father's death. Mrs. H. quarrelled with the clinic psychiatrist working with herself and refused to go on seeing him. She had been unable to let him raise the question of the loss of her husband. However, she was so anxious for Samantha to continue therapy that we agreed to do so, with many misgivings about working without close contact with a parent. Our misgivings were soon justified. It was obvious that, without the chance to check with us personally at the clinic, Mrs. H. was doing her checking outside. Conversations with a psychologist uncle prompted Samantha to say to me, “Harold Lloyd isn't approved of.” An imaginative leap I was rather proud of prompted me to ask, “Do you mean Sigmund Freud?” She did mean Freud, and was conveying to me the doubts in her family circle about the theories and techniques I might be subjecting her to.

Walk-In Work with Adolescents

Anne Hurry

Anne Hurry

51 Winchester Avenue
London, N.W.6

Anne Hurry  

It is generally recognised that our mental health services cannot adequately meet the needs of adolescents, many of whom are unwilling to attend child guidance or family clinics, or are inappropriately placed in adult psychiatric units. A variety of special clinics and advice centres have been set up in an attempt to meet this need, but very little has been published about work in such clinics from a psychoanalytic viewpoint. I am aware of only one article, Jack Novick's “Walk in Clinics for Adolescents”, published in this Journal in 1977.

Novick describes the work of the Brent Consultation Centre* and gives an illuminating account of some counter-transference reactions to adolescents. He notes that most of the adolescents who “walk in” are severely disturbed, for “those adolescents who need only advice and support are perfectly capable of obtaining it from contemporaries or significant adults immediately available to them”. Novick holds that many adolescents come for help when there has been a failure in their long-standing pathological defences, and I believe that this is indeed so. He also holds that the point at which adolescents walk in is the time they are most likely to accept help, and he draws the conclusion that the person the adolescent first sees at the walk-in centre should also be the person who treats the disturbance. At the time his article was published I was in agreement with this last view. Gradually, however, I have come to think that a change of worker from interviewer to therapist is beneficial and preferable. The adolescent's knowledge that psychotherapeutic treatment — should he opt for it — would be with a worker other than the interviewer, can have most positive effects upon what may be accomplished during interviews and upon the crucial initial stages of therapy itself.

In this paper I hope to give you some impression of our work at Brent, although I would refer you to Dr. Novick's article for a more detailed picture of the Centre. I shall refer to some aspects of adolescent pathology and say why I believe a change of worker to be beneficial. Introduction

My experience in this field has been obtained by consultative, group work and counselling undertaken in a residential school for physically disabled children, which I have visited about fortnightly for the past 312 years, and by psychotherapy with two disabled childen seen at the Tavistock Clinic. I have also been greatly assisted by a Study Group, the members of which are child psychotherapists working with handicapped or chronically sick children in a number of settings, special day and residential schools, a residential home, clinics, paediatric wards and hospital departments.

My very limited previous experience in this field had led me to suppose that the physical disabilities were so evident and so distressing that no one could bear to think that these children might also have the hidden disabilites of psychic suffering, like any one else, or possibly more so. Despite a gradual increase of referrals of the physically disabled, this preconception has largely been confirmed rather than refuted by closer acquaintance with this field. I have slowly come to realise that the trauma and mental suffering of the physically disabled are difficult to perceive due to a bewilderment of complex defences which are activated both in the physically disabled and in those who work with them.

In this paper I intend to concentrate mainly upon some difficulties which are likely to be experienced in the counter-transference when we are working with children who have experienced external trauma. I shall make particular reference to what may be learnt from some counter-transference phenomena which may be specific to work with the physically disabled.

Trauma beyond the therapist's experience

As we continue to extend the applications of psychotherapy we are increasingly drawn to work with those who have experienced external traumas in addition to the universal psychic trauma. The universal trauma arise from the losses and changes of normal development, especially those which are experienced as threats to narcissism and omnipotence, closely linking with the traumas and conflicts stemming from inner wishes and fears, the perverse, sadistic and envious desires. Family Scripts: A Concept which can Bridge Child Psychotherapy and Family Therapy Thinking

John Byng-Hall

John Byng-Hall

120 Belsize Lane
London N.W.3

John Byng-Hall  

Introduction

Child psychotherapists and family therapists need to collaborate. Family therapy is now the major therapeutic approach in many child guidance clinics. Interventions are usually briefer and one therapist, if suitably supported, can treat the whole family. The economics of that are powerful and will not go away. Some children, however, do not respond to family therapy but do dramatically well in child psychotherapy. I refer a number of children for child psychotherapy for that reason. My own view is that family work provides a good launching pad for child psychotherapy. The child when released from scapegoating processes is freer to explore and develop in psychotherapy.

Family therapy is not a separate discipline in the UK. It is a skill added to other professional qualifications such as child psychiatry, social work, psychology or child psychology, etc. In my experience child psychotherapists also make excellent family therapists. The other disciplines using family therapy skills have a lot to learn from child psychotherapists about understanding children. Without this ability seeing families can become work with parents in front of the children. Each approach then needs the other.

In this paper I will present the concept of family scripts (Byng-Hall, 1985) which links intrapsychic and interpersonal phenomena and I will show how it was used with a family. Various family therapy interventions will be illustrated in this way.

Family Scripts; their nature

Each member of the family has an “inner family” which helps to determine what goes on in the outer family; just as each member of the cast has a script for a play. Sitting with families one becomes aware of the same basic pattern of interaction, with minor variations, repeated over and over again like the rerun of one scene in a play. The advantage of the concept of script over object relations theory is that it addresses more readily the fact that everyone not only casts every member of the family in their inner world but is simultaneously playing roles in everyone else's scripts. Not surprisingly, however, object relations theory can be readily translated into script terms. Casting of roles, for instance, involves projective identifications, splitting, etc., etc. Understudying is through identification and introjection, and so on.

Miranda Feuchtwang

Miranda Feuchtwang

Miranda Feuchtwang  

The translation into English by Paul Barrows of The Ego Ideal and the publication of Creativity and Perversion, based on the lectures given by Janine Chasseguet-Smirgel as Freud professor at University College, London 1982-83 is timely and much to be welcomed. Chasseguet-Smirgel's concerns are in the best tradition of classical psychoanalytic thought, a reminder that psychoanalysis is more than clinical practice: it is also philosophy, a living Weltanschauung of contemporary pertinence that exists within and is produced by the context of contemporary socio-cultural problems. Since Freud, individual man is both profoundly unconscious, interior and privatised; simultaneously conscious, outer directed and socialised. This constitutes a permanent tension and a dilemma.

Chasseguet-Smirgel's review of Freudian man re-elaborates the tragic/heroic struggle of the helpless and dependent human infant in us all. We are haunted by regressive temptations in the nostalgia for lost narcissism. We live in that tension of the never-to-be breached gap, the ego's retrospective view of lost perfection and its anticipation of future narcissistic satisfaction. The profound narcissistic wound in the ego, installed by separation, birth, weaning, the individuation process itself, is never healed. It admits of two solutions, the one distintegrative in furtherance of splitting processes, the other integrative and developmental. There is the permanent temptation of regressive idealisation versus the developmental solution, the cathexes of sublimated satisfactions which modify, or to add Meltzer's term, may even modulate the narcissistic dilemma of being human.

The key concept in this description is ego ideal as support to the ego; as ideal ego (idealising the narcissistic phantasies and proclivities of the infant) it may lead to perversity, falsity, delusional solutions. It promotes the lie that denies reality, the non recognition of difference, and especially that of difference between the generations, and between the sexes. It is the denial of human procreativity, and the infant's incapacity in this respect. In this perverse world, there is a reduction effectively via omnipotent infantile phantasy to an idealised fecal paradise. But as Chasseguet-Smirgel notes in her introductory chapter (Creavity and Perversion), the perverse, reality disordering, reductive and regressive solution to the pain of recognition of human helplessness and dependency “is a temptation in the mind common to us all”.

Secrecy Surrounding a Pregnancy and its Effect on the Treatment of a Seven-Year-Old Child

Deborah Steiner

Deborah Steiner

120 Belsize Lane
London, NW3

Deborah Steiner  

In this paper I will describe the first year of treatment of a rather narcissistic boy when a fourth child was conceived and born into the family. The mother withheld this news from the child and I will show how I was drawn into the secrecy and deception; and how this had a profound effect on my freedom of movement with the child and on my capacity to help him.

A situation arose in the treatment which reflected elements in the family dynamics, and which prevented Alex (as I shall call him) from working through his oedipal difficulties and contributed to his learning problems. The child himself had a propensity for tricky and deceptive behaviour, and a suspicious and tricky atmosphere came to pervade the treatment and was evident in his material. I became identified with both the deceiving mother who colluded with the child's oedipal fantasies, and with a weak father who was unable to help him with the problematic and involved relationship with his mother. This boy used defences of omnipotent denial, omniscience and pseudo-maturity to sustain his oedipal fantasies. I will show how these were threatened by the pregnancy itself and by the way the knowledge of the pregnancy was used.

The family

The D. family was middle-class and Jewish and the parents presented as caring and attentive, with firm ideas about how children should be brought up. They had no television, and comics and guns were forbidden. Great emphasis was placed on academic achievement, and although I did not have the impression that this was excessive, there was more pressure on my patient, Alex, in this and other respects as the oldest and only son. For example, he went to a somewhat rigid and striving Jewish school, while his two sisters attended a more relaxed local authority school. Alex was expected to be grown up and polite and this led to a neglect of his infantile needs. For instance, when the new baby arrived Alex was moved from his room and given a corner of a downstairs room where Mrs. D. ran a playgroup, and while the parents made a great effort to make it his special corner with a bunk-bed/cupboard arrangement, Mrs. D. insisted to me that Alex was very pleased with it and did not mind giving up his room to the baby.
